competition_series: FSAE Michigan (primary, annual); Formula Student Germany (FSG, Driverless Cup, first entered 2025); Formula Student Czech (2023)
summary: UTFR (est. 1997, formerly a 23-year combustion program) pivoted to an all-electric car in 2022, skipped competing that year to focus preparation, then returned in 2023 with UT23 and won its first overall FSAE Michigan podium result since 2006 (5th overall) plus 6th at FS Czech. The driverless program began layering onto this EV platform with EBS validation in November 2023, reached full autonomous navigation of the Acceleration and AutoX courses by November 2024, and became the first and only team to pass all inspections and run a fully autonomous autocross demonstration at FSAE Michigan 2025. Later that season UTFR became the first North American team to compete in FSG's Driverless Cup, reaching the Driverless Design Finals and placing 7th of 42 teams in its debut driverless year (per the team's own recap; FSG's aggregate scoring table shows 44th of 84 at FS DE 2025 overall). UTFR is a same-climate, same-academic-calendar Canadian peer whose driverless ramp (roughly EBS-validation to full-course autonomy in about a year, program-conception to first driverless competition entry in about 2-2.5 years) is the closest available analog to a Winnipeg-based team building on an existing EV platform. Public technical detail on sensor models, compute hardware, and cost is thin; most of what is documented comes from a single team recap video/post and secondary press rather than a technical design report.
dv_program_start: [uncertain] Approximately 2022-early 2023. A 2025 team recap states the driverless build began 'over two years' before UTFR's FSAE Michigan 2025 autonomous demonstration, and the earliest dated driverless milestone found is EBS validation in November 2023, implying design/formation work started in 2022 or very early 2023, in parallel with the team's 2022 EV pivot.

first_dv_competition: FSAE Michigan 2025 (first driverless-class dynamic demonstration, passed all driverless tech inspections and ran an autonomous autocross demo) and Formula Student Germany 2025 (first formal Driverless Cup entry, Driverless Design Finalist, 1st North American team ever to compete in FSG's Driverless Cup).

months_concept_to_first_competition: [uncertain] approximately 24-30 months (2022/early-2023 start to the FSAE Michigan / FSG driverless entries in mid-2025).
months_to_first_scoring_run: [uncertain] approximately 24 months to the November 2024 'full autonomous navigation of Acceleration and AutoX courses' milestone, and roughly 30 months to the first scored competition driverless dynamic event in 2025.

ramp_phases: Informally inferable rather than formally named by the team: (1) EV platform pivot (2022), (2) driverless architecture stand-up + partial-scope capability limited to Acceleration/Skidpad (2023, ~12 months), (3) hardware/software validation sprint — EBS validation Nov 2023, full EBS on car May 2024, remote e-stop June 2024, system validation July 2024, perception improvements Sept 2024 (roughly 10 months of dated validation milestones), (4) first full-course autonomy, Nov 2024, (5) first competition season with driverless entries, 2025 (UT25), (6) platform pivot to 4WD EV with driverless status unclear, 2026.
what_slipped: [uncertain] No explicit team statement of a schedule slip was found, but several soft signals exist: (1) the team scoped 2023 driverless capability down to only Acceleration and Skidpad rather than full autocross, implying the original full-course ambition slipped by roughly a year to November 2024; (2) the ~8-9 month gap between 'full EBS on vehicle' (May 2024) and 'full autonomous navigation' (November 2024) suggests integration/software issues consumed most of a season; (3) FSAE Michigan overall ranking fell from 5th (2023) to 10th (2024) to 15th (2025) to 51st (2026), coincident with driverless and then 4WD development, suggesting DV (and later 4WD) work absorbed resources at the expense of base-vehicle competitiveness; (4) the 2026 season-kickoff communication omits driverless entirely, a possible signal that the DV program stalled or was deprioritized after the 2025 FSG debut.
platform_prerequisites: Yes. UTFR built its driverless system on top of an already-running EV platform: the 2022 EV pivot (UT22/UT23 development) preceded any documented driverless milestone, and the team's first driverless capability (2023) was layered onto the freshly competitive UT23 EV car rather than requiring a from-scratch EV conversion concurrently with driverless work.

critical_path_items: Based on the dated milestone sequence: (1) EBS hardware validation and full-vehicle EBS integration (Nov 2023 to May 2024, ~6 months) as the clear long pole before any autonomous testing could proceed under FSAE safety rules; (2) closing the gap from full EBS integration to full autonomous navigation (May-Nov 2024, ~6 months) which likely reflects perception/planning/control software maturation as the second critical path item; (3) building a competitive EV base platform each year (UT23-UT25) in parallel with driverless work, given the team's overall FSAE Michigan ranking degraded across 2023-2026 coincident with driverless and 4WD development, suggesting resource contention between base-vehicle and driverless/advanced-powertrain work is itself a critical-path constraint for a small team.

team_structure_dv: Per UTFR's 2025-2026 Team Constitution, Driverless is one of three formal engineering sections (alongside Mechanical and Electrical) reporting to the Technical Director(s), who in turn report to the Team Principal; a separate Business Director runs finance/sponsorship. Overall team size is 90-120+ active contributors across all sections (90 reported in the Sept 2025 season-kickoff newsletter; 120+ reported in a 2023-2024-era team description), with driverless-specific headcount not broken out in any source found. Named driverless technical leads for the 2023-2024 development cycle: Kelvin Cui, Daniel Asadi, and Youssef Elhadad.

A 2025 crowdfunding campaign sought $10,000 CAD (raised $7,500) specifically to help cover 'competition registration, shipping the car overseas, tools and spares, and on-site operations' for the Michigan + Germany double-competition season, which is a partial proxy for incremental cross-continental competition costs but not a driverless system build cost.
recommended_sequence: Synthesized from UTFR's dated milestone order (not team-stated as an explicit sequence): (1) get a competitive EV base platform running first and prove it in EV-class competition (UTFR did this in 2022-2023 before layering on driverless); (2) build and validate the EBS as a standalone subsystem before attempting any vehicle-level autonomous testing (UTFR: Nov 2023 standalone EBS validation, ~6 months before full vehicle EBS integration in May 2024); (3) validate the full safety chain - EBS on vehicle, then remote emergency stop, then a comprehensive system validation - as three distinct, sequential gates before pursuing higher-level autonomy (UTFR: May, June, July 2024 respectively); (4) scope the first season's autonomous capability narrowly (e.g., Acceleration/Skidpad only, straight-line and low-speed maneuvers) before attempting full autocross/trackdrive autonomy, and treat 'pass tech inspection and complete one clean autonomous run' as the first season's real success metric rather than a competitive placing.
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: UTFR is the single most structurally comparable case in this study: same country-adjacent winter climate, same academic-year calendar, a similarly sized student-run FSAE team, and - critically - UTFR built its driverless system on top of an already-running, competition-proven EV platform, exactly matching a Winnipeg team's assumed starting point. UTFR's own timeline (EBS validated ~Nov 2023, full autonomous navigation ~Nov 2024, first driverless competition entries mid-2025) suggests that roughly 24-30 months from a standing EV platform to a first driverless competition entry is achievable but not generous - it matches the proposed June 2026-June 2028 window almost exactly, with limited slack. The most important applicable lessons: (a) do not attempt full-course autonomy in year one - scope the first season to Acceleration/Skidpad-equivalent low-speed capability, as UTFR did in 2023; (b) treat the EBS-validate to full-vehicle-EBS-integrate step as a hard ~6-month gate before any autonomous driving attempt, matching UTFR's Nov 2023-May 2024 timeline; (c) beware resource contention - UTFR's overall vehicle competitiveness (FSAE Michigan ranking) declined across the same years its driverless program ramped and then declined further when it added a 4WD powertrain overhaul on top, a caution against a ~9-person software-focused DV team also being expected to prop up base-vehicle performance; (d) the payoff for persistence is real - UTFR went from zero driverless competition history to first North American FSG Driverless Cup entrant and FSAE Michigan's only passing driverless demo team within about 2.5 years, which is a credible existence proof for a comparable 24-month target, provided the team does not also take on a major concurrent base-vehicle redesign.
